indexing.name: Index Villaris, 1680
indexing.description: 'INDEX VILLARIS: or, An Alphabetical Table of all the cities, market-towns, parishes, villages, and private seats in England and Wales' was first published by John Adams in 1680. This dataset transcribes all 24,000 entries (title, county and hundred as printed, Adams's latitude and longitude, and his symbols) and adds an editorial layer: the county and hundred meant, a point, and links to CAMPOP Places, Wikidata and GB1900. Points are OpenStreetMap nodes chosen by hand (© OpenStreetMap contributors, Geocoding Results under the OSMF Geocoding Guideline) or, for places corrected in v2.1.0, the coordinates of their Wikidata item. Cities and market towns are typed and linked to CAMPOP Places.

contributions.notes: Tentative.  Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 has a settlement here called 'Anter Chester' https://maps.nls.uk/view/104188207  Armstrong's map of 1769 has a hill fort called 'Turn Chester' but at a location a few miles north west of here. This is probably an error as that location is not in the high ground. http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79584  The linked site appears to be the only place in the area with the name 'Chester(s)', but if 'Anter Chester' is referring to a hill fort, there are numerous other hill forts in the area, mostly unnamed on OS maps. (D King)

The County History of Northumberland vol 11, p 187, identifies 'Anter Chester' with 'Thompsons Walls', although acknowledges some degree of uncertainty. https://archive.org/details/historyofnorthum11nort/page/186/mode/1up?q=chester  While 'Anter Chester' is recorded on the Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 'Thompsons Walls' is not.  Conversely, 'Thomsons Walls' is recorded on Armstrongs map of 1769, but 'Anter Chester' is not. http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79584 (D King)

contributions.notes: Added this further possibility to recognise the association of Nether Blacklaw with this location. Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 has a Blaklaw on the River Rede slightly to the east of here https://maps.nls.uk/view/104188207 Armstrong's map of 1769 has a High & Low Blacklaw here https://maps.nls.uk/view/220113124 Blakelaw on the 1st edition OS 6" is probably the Low Blacklaw of Armstrong, while Hightown to the north is probably Armstrong's High Blacklaw These can't be ruled out for Over & Nether Blacklaw, as they are also in the old  Simonburn parish.

Possibly Blacklaw, shown as a 'seat' on the Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 https://maps.nls.uk/view/104188207 although the location is a little confused. Northumberland place names cites a 1348 record of Blaclawe in Simonburn parish, which would tally with the 1662-5 map.  https://altogetherarchaeology.org/Place%20Names/PLACE-NAMES%20OF%20NORTHUMBERLAND%20AND%20DURHAM.pdf Armstrong's map of 1769 however appears not to have a Blacklaw close to Simonburn, but has both a place name & a burn called Blacklaw Burn which tally with the place & burn which are now called Blackaburn https://maps.nls.uk/view/102346422  Hodgson, History of Northumberland Part III vol 1, p309 has a list of ratepayers dated 1809, but including corresponding records for 1663, in which are included Nether Blacklaw & Over Blacklaw in Simonburn parish. I think there is no doubt that this placename is Over Blacklaw, and it is in Simonburn parish, but I am not totally convinced that this is the correct location within that parish - which was a very large parish.

contributions.notes: Tentative at best, but there is a Carr House at Great Bavington, although I have yet to find any related old records. Northumberland Quarter Sessions records have one 1603 record of the place name Carhowses, not yet located. https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/99b7e6af-0a28-46c7-ac9d-446961e2a69d (D King)

This is a much better prospect. Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 locates Carehouse at approx this location https://maps.nls.uk/view/104188207 Armstrong's map of 1769 has Carry House here Whether the location is High or Low Carry House I am not clear, but the record of a Bastle at High Carry House might suggest it is the older of the two http://www.gatehouse-gazetteer.info/English%20sites/2427.html The Northumberland County History, vol 4 p356 mentions a survey of Birtley dated 1586 and "Thomas  Harbottle,  who  held  a  'parcel  of  demeyne ground  called  Caryhowse'  with  a  mansion  house  well  builded  thereon,  at  the rent  of  £5  and  16d" https://archive.org/details/historyofnorthum04nort/page/356  (D King)

contributions.notes: Very tentative.  Not shown on either Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 or Armstrong's map of 1769.  There are 19C burials at Knarsdale 'of Church Stile', and the 1st edition OS 6" map, surveyed 1861, shows 'The Church Style' public house. (D King)

Although reliant on accepting that Kirkstile was also known as Churchstile, support for the Whitfield version comes from a deed at Northumberland Archives (NRO324/W/1/9) dated 1699, between John Whitfield of The Kirkstile senior & John Whitfield of the same, junr, and Nicholas Whitfield of the Kirkstile, yeoman referring to a messuage or tenement called Kirkstile (D King)

Very tentative.  Not found on either Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 or Armstrong's map of 1769.  County History of Northumberland, vol 4 p120 notes the mention of Nicholas Whitfield of Churchstile in an inventory of 1699 https://www.electricscotland.com/northumberland/historyofnorthum04nort.pdf  Also, an 18C survey of Whitfield is said to include the rental of 10 fields at Church Stile http://www.dickinsons-of-whitfield.org/Whitfield.html (D King)

contributions.notes: A further option in Bamburgh Ward is Easington Grange.  Not marked on Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5  Marked as 'Grange' on Armstrong's map of 1769 http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79584  'Easington Grange' on the 1st edition OS 6"  Ths County History of Northumberland, vol 1, p362 deals briefly with Easington Grange, but does note that it is known as 'the Grange'. (D King)

Grange is such a generic name on its own, everything will be tentative. However..  Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 does not have the name 'Grange' anywhere in Bamburgh Ward.  'Heckley Grange' is the closest to the current prospective location.  Armstrong's map  of 1769 names only 'Grange' at this location https://maps.nls.uk/view/220113127  1st edition OS 6" (https://maps.nls.uk/view/102346296) shows a large building called 'Heckley Grange' at the selected location to the east of Heckley House, which has disappeared from this edition.    The County History of Northumberland vol 1, p189 mentions John Younghusband of 'Grange near Alnwick', two of whose sons were of 'Heckley Grange', almost certainly the same place  NOTE: Heckley Grange is on the edge of Coquetdale Ward, and thus is perhaps less likely than 'Easington Grange' to be 'this' grange.   (D King)

contributions.notes: Tentative.  Housesteads is the only place in Tindale Ward which remotely resembles this name. I have no other evidence for it.  It was named as 'Housesteads' on the 1769 map of Armstrong, http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79588 (D King)

While the name 'Heesteds' might reasonably be thought to be a corruption of 'High Stead(s)', this Northumberland example is not in Tindale Ward, nor can I find any indication it is an old site or name. (D King)

Armstrong's map of 1769 has a house called 'High Steeds' at approx this location http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79587  The County History of Northumberland, vol 15, p238 has an ?undated (?18C) list of the farms in Nook Township as including 'High Stead'  This place not listed in a list of farms in Nook dated 1618/23, and cannot be found on the 1st edition OS 6". (D King)

contributions.notes: Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 has a settlement called 'Hoclugh' at approx this location.  However, neither Armstrong's map of 1769, or the 1st edition OS show this name. (D King)

In Archaeoligia Aeliana, series 3, vol 4 p142 the following is noted, (drawing also on AA ser 2, vol 14 p45):   "In the view of border fortalices drawn up by Sir Robert Bowes and Sir Ralph Ellerker in 1541, a, structure in the imme diate neighbourhood of the towers of Barrow and Great Tosson is described in the following words: ‘ At a place called the hareclewgh one Rogr Hangingeshawes hath lately buylded upon his owne Inherytance a stronge pele house of stone in a convenyent place for resystence of the Incourse of theves of Ryddesdayle, and he ys not able in defaulte of substance to performe & fynyshe the same’   This seems a possible reason for the name appearing in the 16C but not later.   However, the case is somewhat confused as the Hangingshawe family also had links for some time to Harehaugh, an enduring settlement a couple of miles downstream, and which also appears in this list & on early maps.   While the suffix 'clewgh' (later Cleugh) is and was entirely distinct from the suffix 'haugh', historians seem to have struggled to clarify whether or not 'hareclewgh' was a separate place based only upon a single 16C source, and it is entirely possible that the place named 'Hoclugh' by Speed & Blaeu didn't exist, and was based upon a misunderstanding of names? (D King)

(extract https://co-curate.ncl.ac.uk/leemailing-township-1848/) identifies it as a 'township' at this location, included within which is Hesleyside. (D King)

contributions.notes: Nook was a township within Bellingham parish, see Kelly's directory of 1894: "Nook, formerly a separate township, was amalgamated in 1886, under the Divided Parishes Act, with Bellingham and Wark parishes: it is half a mile east from Bellingham, consisting of a few detached farms, on the west bank of the river Reed and on the north bank of the North Tyne"  This location tallies with the approximate location given in Speed (1610) & Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5, although they both appear to have the positions of Blaklaw & Nuke transposed from their current locations.  It does not appear on Armstrong's map of 1769.  There does not appear to be any remnant of a settlement as such, although early 19C records mention a Nook Mill, I cannot locate it even on the 1st edition OS 6" (D King)

contributions.notes: A house to the west of Newcastle which belonged in the 17C to the prominent families of Anderson & Jenison.  A survey of Elswick of 1608 includes a newly erected house etc in a place called the Quarries, without the Westgate by Bartram Anderson. A History of Northumberland, vol 13, p 245  p 249 of the above notes that Quarry House had descended to Bertram Anderson, was sequestered in 1646, and was bought by Sir Ralph Jenison.  A map of 1746 "To William His Royal Highness Duke of Cumberland This Plan of Newcastle upon Tyne is humbly dedicated By his Royal Highnes's most obedient devoted Servant Isaac Thompson 1746" shows Quarry House at this location. https://www.flickr.com/photos/britishlibrary/50264384648  It does not appear on the 1st edition OS 6" as this location has become part of the 19C development of the west end of Newcastle. (D King)

contributions.notes: If this name is referring to Shotley, which seems likely although Shotley was in Tindale Ward, this alternative location is the site of the church, there was no village as such, large areas of dispersed settlement given the name Shotley High Quarter & Shotley Low Quarter.  Speed (1610) & Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 have 'Shotley' by the river, and the word 'Bridge', which is not clear whether it represents Shotley Bridge, or whether the word Bridge just shows there is a bridge there.  To confuse the issue, both Speed (1610) & Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 https://maps.nls.uk/view/104188207 show a place called 'Shorley' a few miles to the NW. I can find no suitable place name on either Armstrong or the 1st edition OS 6", nor in the County History vol 6 which covers this parish. I am inclined to think that this is supposed to represent the church at some distance from the river, albeit if that is the case, then it has been placed too far to the NW on the other side of the settlement called 'Farley'.  Armstrong's map of 1769 separately names 'Shotley Bridge', 'Shotley Hall' near the bridge, 'Shotley Field' which may have been an original settlement, and also the church of Shotley. http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79588

In addition, Archaeologia Aeliana, vol 21, p125  https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archiveDS/archiveDownload?t=arch-3433-1/dissemination/AASeries2/AA221new/archael221-000-000-PDFs/archael221-083-145-terry_charles.pdf reports a letter of 1646 which includes the phrase "..Towns of Walker, Wamson, and Willington.."

contributions.notes: Northumberland Archives, deed (NRO324/W/1/9) dated 21.1.1679 between John Whitfield of Wall, Northumberland, slater and Utrick Whitfield of Whitfield Hall regarding a moiety of a customary tenement called Winnels Raw als Winless Raw (D King)
Horsley's map of 1753 shows 'The Raw' at approx this location, between Parmentley and Owston and to the west of the road. (D King)

Exact location uncertain.  Blaeu Atlas Maior 1662-5 has a settlement called Winnelrau at approximately this location https://maps.nls.uk/view/104188207  The London Magazine, Or, Gentleman's Monthly Intelligencer,  vol 17 (1748) p440 has a map showing Winnelraw between Whitfield & Ouston (https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/The_London_Magazine_Or_Gentleman_s_Month/YfsRAAAAYAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22winnelraw%22+northumberland&pg=PA440-IA1&printsec=frontcover)  Also recorded in A Book of the Names of All Parishes, Market Towns, Villages ... in England and Wales ... (1677) (https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/A_Book_of_the_Names_of_All_Parishes_Mark/MOVCAQAAMAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0)   & The The Universal Gazetteer of 1807 (https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/The_universal_gazetteer/C2gDAAAAQAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0)   Armstrong's map of 1769 does not record anything resembling this name in this area. http://digitalarchive.mcmaster.ca/islandora/object/macrepo%3A79588  There is a brief reference in Hodgson's History of Northumberland, part 2, vol 3, p99, to Winnels Raw being a customary tenement of the Whitfield Estate. (D King)
